lessons.title: sein — "to be"
lessons.gloss: to be — the partner of haben, and the most irregular verb German has

segments.text: You have met the German verb for to have. Here is its partner — the most irregular verb in German, and the one verb whose forms you will not be able to guess.
sein — "to be."
The -en on the end is the infinitive ending you already own from gehen and sehen: the dictionary form of a German verb wears it, and sein wears it too.
That is where the resemblance stops. Gehen and sehen keep their stem in every form — ich gehe, ich sehe. Sein keeps nothing. Not one of its present forms contains the letters s-e-i-n in that order.

This is the only verb in the book that has to be met one form at a time, and the next several lessons do exactly that: one form each, said until it is automatic, before any of them are ever seen side by side.
s-voiced — a German s before a vowel buzzes like English z, exactly as it does in sehen. So sein opens with a z.
diphthong-ei — German ei is the vowel of English eye, never "ee".
final-t — worth having ready now, because two of the forms coming up end in a crisp, fully released t.
Put together, sein sounds like English zine.

segments.instruction: "sein" (zine) — buzzing z, ei as in eye
"gehen, sehen, sein" — three infinitives, one ending
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "gehen, sehen, sein" — three infinitives, one ending]

segments.text: "sein, sein — zine."

What does sein mean? ("To be.") Which ending does it share with gehen and sehen? (-en, the infinitive.) How does the s sound? (Like English z.) And the ei? (Like English eye.) Next: the first form, and it looks nothing like the word you just learned.

lessons.title: ich bin — "I am"
lessons.gloss: I am — the first form of sein, and it comes from a different verb than the infinitive does

segments.text: You have ich, and you have the infinitive sein. Put them together and you get a form that shares no letters with either half of that sentence except the i.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: ich bin

segments.text: ich bin — "I am."
One syllable, short i, ordinary b, ordinary n. There is no rule behind it and nothing to derive it from: bin is simply the form that goes with ich, and it is learned the way you learned hallo.
It rhymes with English bin, and that rhyme is not an accident — see below.
ich-laut — ich still ends in the soft breathy sound you met when you first said "I": tongue where it sits for ee, air pushed past it, no scrape.
i-short — the i of bin is short and clipped, the vowel of English bin, not the long ee of ihm.
Bin rhymes with English be for a reason, even though the vowels have drifted apart. Both come from Proto-Indo-European bʰuH- — "to grow, to become."

So German kept that ancient root in the present tense and English kept it as the infinitive: be and bin are the same old word wearing different jobs. Hold on to that; two lessons from now it explains something about the whole verb.

segments.instruction: "ich bin" — short i, soft ending on ich
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ich bin" — short *i*, soft ending on *ich*]
[YOU SAY: "bin — be" — the same old root]

segments.text: "ich bin, ich bin."
Say "I am." (Ich bin.) Is the i of bin long or short? (Short — English bin.) Which English word comes from the same root as bin? (Be.) Next: the same verb for the person you are talking to.

lessons.title: du bist — "you are"
lessons.gloss: you are — bin plus the -st ending you already know, and the one place sein behaves

segments.text: Du is the familiar "you" — the one for a friend. Its verb ending is -st, and for once sein uses it.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: du bist

segments.text: du bist — "you are."
Take bin, drop the n, add the familiar -st: bi- plus -st is bist. That is the same ending as du gehst, du heißt, du siehst.
Of the six present forms of sein, this is the only one that can be derived from another one. Enjoy it; it does not happen again.
u-long — du has a long, rounded oo, the vowel of English do, held.
final-t — German releases a final t fully and audibly. Bist ends with a small puff of air; English tends to swallow it.

segments.instruction: "du bist" — long u, crisp final t

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ich bin … du bist" — the pair]

segments.text: "ich bin, du bist."

Say "you are," to a friend. (Du bist.) Which ending is that? (-st, the familiar one.) Which form is bist built on? (Bin.) Is the final t released or swallowed? (Released.) Next: the form for everybody else.

lessons.title: er ist — "he is"
lessons.gloss: he is — the form that also serves sie, es and das, and the one that matches Latin est

segments.text: Bin and bist both start with b. The third form does not, and it is the one you will hear most.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: er ist

segments.text: er ist — "he is."
er is "he." The same ist serves three more subjects without changing at all: sie ist ("she is"), es ist ("it is"), and das ist ("that is") — es and das both already yours.
So one two-letter word covers everything that is not ich and not du, in the singular. It is the workhorse of the whole verb.
r-final — the r at the end of er is not a full English r. It softens towards a vowel, close to air said without the tongue curling.
final-t — ist ends in the same released t as bist.
Ist is the one form of sein whose relatives you can name on sight:
All from Proto-Indo-European h₁es-, "to be" — and the infinitive sein is built on that root too. So sein and ist really do belong to each other; it is bin and bist that came from somewhere else.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "er ist, sie ist, es ist"]
[YOU SAY: "ich bin, du bist, er ist"]

segments.text: "Das ist gut."
Say "he is." (Er ist.) Which other subjects take the same form? (Sie, es, das.) Say "that is good." (Das ist gut.) Which Latin word is ist? (Est.) Next: the form for more than one.

lessons.title: wir sind — "we are"
lessons.gloss: we are — the plural form, and the first one that looks like the infinitive

segments.text: Three singular forms down. The plural starts here, and after bin, bist, ist, this one will finally look like the verb it belongs to.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: wir sind

segments.text: wir sind — "we are."
wir is "we." And sind shares its first two letters with the infinitive sein, which is the first visible family resemblance in this verb.
Its Latin twin is sunt, "they are" — same s, same n, same closing stop, the same root wearing a different vowel.
w-as-v — German w is English v. Wir begins like veer.
ie-long-ee — ie is a long ee. Wir is veer, not wire.
d-t-final — the d at the end of sind is spoken as a t, the same final devoicing you met on und. Say zint.

segments.instruction: "wir sind" — veer zint, final d as t

segments.text: "wir sind, wir sind."
Say "we are." (Wir sind.) How is the final d pronounced? (As a t.) How does wir begin? (Like English v.) Which Latin word is sind? (Sunt.) Next: the plural "you."

lessons.title: ihr seid — "you are," to several people
lessons.gloss: you are, to more than one person — the form English lost when it dropped its plural you

segments.text: Du is one friend. For two or more friends German has a separate word, and English used to have one as well.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: ihr seid

segments.text: ihr seid — "you are," said to more than one person you would each call du.

ihr is the familiar plural "you" — a crowd of friends, a group of children, your own family. English once had ye here and let it go, which is why one English you now does the work of four German words.
seid opens exactly like the infinitive: sei- is sein without its n. Both the s and the ei behave as they did there.
ie-long-ee — ihr is eer, one long vowel; the h only stretches it.
s-voiced — seid opens with the buzzing z of sein.
diphthong-ei — and carries the eye vowel through. Say zite.
Wir sind and ihr seid are the two plural forms, and they sound nothing alike, which makes them easy to keep apart.
"ihr seid, ihr seid."

Say "you are" to a group of friends. (Ihr seid.) Which English word did that job before English dropped it? (Ye.) Which part of seid comes straight out of sein? (sei-.) Next: the last form, and the one that does double duty.

lessons.title: sie sind / Sie sind — "they are," and "you are," politely
lessons.gloss: they are, and the polite you are — one form, and the capital letter is the only difference

segments.text: The polite Sie is literally the word for "they," worn as a courtesy. Its verb form follows from that, and costs you nothing new.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: sie sind and Sie sind

segments.text: sie sind — "they are." Sie sind — "you are," to someone you would address formally.
The form is sind, the very same word you learned for wir. Nothing changes in the mouth at all: wir sind, sie sind, Sie sind are three subjects and one verb form.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the capital carries the politeness

segments.text: On the page, sie and Sie differ by exactly one capital letter — and German already spends capitals on grammar rather than decoration. In speech there is no difference at all; the context tells you which one is meant.

utterances: Sie sind means you are, formally.

segments.text: That is the whole of it. Six subjects, and you have now met every present form of the verb.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Sie sind Herr Peter Schmidt?" — politely]

segments.instruction: "wir sind, sie sind, Sie sind" — one form, three subjects
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "wir sind, sie sind, Sie sind" — one form, three subjects]

segments.text: "sie sind, Sie sind."

Say "they are." (Sie sind.) Say "you are" to a stranger. (Sie sind — same sound.) What separates the two on paper? (The capital S.) How many different present forms of this verb have you now met? (Five — bin, bist, ist, sind, seid.) Next: one adjective, so you can finally say something about yourself.

lessons.title: müde — "tired"
lessons.gloss: tired — the first adjective that says something about a person, and it needs no ending here

segments.text: Ich bin is a sentence waiting for one more word. Here is the word that finishes it most often.
müde — "tired."
Ich bin müde. — "I am tired."

Two syllables, stress on the first: mü-duh. It is an adjective, and after sein an adjective takes no ending at all — the same bare form serves every subject. Ich bin müde, du bist müde, wir sind müde.
That is worth noticing, because German adjectives are famous for their endings. They only take them in front of a noun. Standing after sein, they stand still.

umlaut-ue — ü is the vowel you make by rounding your lips for oo and then saying ee without moving them. The dots are the fronting mark you already know: the mouth shifts forward, the lips stay round.
The final -e is a soft uh, never silent. mü-duh, two beats, the weight on the first.

segments.instruction: "Er ist müde. Wir sind müde." — the adjective never changes
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Er ist müde. Wir sind müde." — the adjective never changes]

segments.text: "Ich bin müde."

Say "I am tired." (Ich bin müde.) How do you make the ü? (Round for oo, say ee.) Does müde change after sein? (No — no ending.) Say "we are tired." (Wir sind müde.) Next: everything at once, on purpose.

lessons.title: Practice — the whole present of sein
lessons.gloss: chapter payoff — the six forms of sein side by side for the first time, and a conversation that uses them

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: No new words. Every form below has had its own lesson, so this is the first time it is safe to put them all on one page — as a recap, not as something to memorise from cold.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the six forms, assembled

utterances: singular: ich bin. plural: wir sind.
singular: du bist. plural: ihr seid.
singular: er/sie/es ist. plural: sie/Sie sind.

segments.text: Six subjects, five different forms — sind does double duty. Look at that with fresh eyes now that you can say all of it: bin and ist do not look like forms of the same word, and the next chapter explains why they aren't.

utterances: Hallo! Wie geht es dir? means Hello! How are you?
Danke, ich bin müde. means Thanks — I am tired.
Du bist müde? Ich auch. means You are tired? Me too.
Dann sind wir müde. Aber das ist gut. means Then we are tired. But that is good.
Bis morgen! means See you tomorrow!

segments.text: Three small joining words slip in there without needing lessons of their own, because each can be read straight off the translation: auch ("too"), dann ("then") and aber ("but").

segments.instruction: the six in order — "ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the six in order — "ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind"]

segments.instruction: "Ich bin müde." "Du bist müde." "Wir sind müde."
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Ich bin müde." "Du bist müde." "Wir sind müde."]
[YOU SAY: the whole exchange, both voices]

segments.text: "ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind."

Run the six forms without looking. Which one form covers wir, sie and Sie? (Sind.) Which is the only form built out of another one? (Bist, from bin.) Say "that is good." (Das ist gut.) Say "you are tired" to a group. (Ihr seid müde.) Next: where these forms came from — three different verbs, none of them each other.
